result.summary: Acheloüs, a river god, tells Theseus how he lost a horn. He and Hercules both sought Deïanira's hand, and Hercules beat him in a wrestling match even though Acheloüs changed into a serpent and then a bull. The Naiads made the broken horn the Horn of Plenty, and the company parts at dawn.

scenes.title: Prologue: the contest and the horn
scenes.summary: The argument summarizes the contest for Deïanira, Acheloüs' defeat and the origin of the Horn of Plenty. Theseus asks Acheloüs why he sighs and why his brow is maimed.

scenes.title: The suitors quarrel and wrestle
scenes.summary: Acheloüs recalls asking Œneus for Deïanira, and insults Hercules' parentage. Hercules answers that his hand beats his tongue, and they begin to wrestle.
scenes.stakes: Acheloüs risks losing Deïanira and his honour in a fight with Hercules.

scenes.title: Defeat and the serpent
scenes.summary: Hercules throws Acheloüs down, so he turns into a serpent. Hercules mocks him, citing the Lernæan hydra, and chokes him.
scenes.stakes: Acheloüs is being overpowered and choked, and may be killed.

scenes.title: The bull and the broken horn
scenes.summary: Acheloüs turns into a bull, but Hercules fells him and tears off a horn. The Naiads fill it with fruit and flowers.
scenes.stakes: Acheloüs loses the fight and a horn.

scenes.title: Fruit, dawn and departure
scenes.summary: A nymph brings the horn full of fruit. At dawn the young men leave, and Acheloüs hides his injury under waves and reeds.
scenes.stakes: Acheloüs grieves over his lost honour.

alias_notes.explanation: Refers to Tiryns, his home city.
Theseus was reputed to be a son of Neptune.

notable_quotes.reason: Hercules' blunt retort, 'My right hand is better than my tongue.'
Acheloüs' dignified claim that glory lies in having fought a mighty conqueror.

analysis.text: The wrestling contest shows pride, honour and shape-changing cunning losing to brute strength. Acheloüs' tale of a wound explains the origin of the Horn of Plenty.
The story is an aetiological myth that explains a cultural symbol. It may also reflect the Achelous river's flooding and the Greeks' attempts to control it.

legacy.text: The cornucopia, or Horn of Plenty, became a lasting symbol of abundance in art and heraldry, and is now associated with Thanksgiving imagery.

fun_facts.text: The Achelous is the longest river in Greece, and ancient writers often linked its twisting course and bull-like roar to this myth.

language_notes.text: Theseus, 'the Neptunian hero', is called so because tradition made Neptune his father (alternatively Aegeus). The Calydonian river is Acheloüs, who flowed near Calydon in Aetolia.
'Son of Parthaon' means Œneus, king of Calydon; Parthaon was his father. Ovid uses the patronymic as a formal address.
Alcides is Hercules, named after his grandfather Alcaeus.
The 'labours' are the twelve tasks Hercules performed, imposed by Eurystheus at Juno's hostile prompting; the 'step-mother' is Juno.
Acheloüs alludes to the story that Jupiter seduced Alcmena by disguising himself as her husband Amphitryon, so Hercules' birth was adulterous.
Hands 'bent inwards' means held up in a guarded wrestling stance, protecting the chest.
Wrestlers sprinkled dust or sand on themselves and each other to get a better grip; hence Hercules turns yellow.
Alcides is a name for Hercules, from his grandfather Alcaeus.
The Tirynthian means Hercules, who was associated with the city of Tiryns.
Hercules strangled two serpents sent by Juno while he was still an infant in his cradle.
The Lernæan hydra, a many-headed water serpent, was killed by Hercules as one of his labours. Ovid here calls it Echidna.
Hercules taunts that Acheloüs' serpent shape is borrowed, a gift of his own shape-changing, and so is a disguise and not his true form.
The horn becomes the cornucopia, the horn of plenty, symbol of abundance. Plenty is personified as a goddess.
Girt up after the manner of Diana means her robe is belted high for hunting, as the huntress goddess is shown.
Fruit for a second course means dessert, which in Roman dining was the fruit that ended a meal.

context_notes.text: Deïanira later became Hercules' wife and, unwittingly, caused his death with the poisoned shirt of Nessus, told later in Book 9.
Juno hated Hercules as the child of her husband's affair, and she set his labours against him. Acheloüs presents her lack of hatred as a point in his favour.
Naiads are freshwater nymphs of rivers, springs and lakes, so they are natural attendants of the river god Acheloüs.
Acheloüs is a river god. His rustic features and horns reflect the river's winding, bull-like roar and branching streams.

literary_notes.text: Acheloüs claims defeat is no disgrace, yet his need to justify himself shows wounded pride.
Hercules' scowl and blunt retort show a man of action who despises words, contrasting with the talkative river-god.
Acheloüs compares himself to a sea-breakwater battered by waves, stressing his massive, immovable bulk.
The wrestling gods are compared to bulls fighting over the finest heifer, which makes the contest an animal struggle for a prize.
Feeling weighed down by a mountain exaggerates Hercules' strength, and the narrator's pledge of honesty adds a note of boasting.
Hercules mocks Acheloüs' serpent form by comparing it to the hydra and to the serpents of his cradle, belittling the transformation.
The tale explains the origin of the cornucopia, turning a loss in a wrestling match into a lasting symbol of plenty.
Acheloüs hides his wound and is troubled only by lost honour, which shows his pride and vanity.
